new_statements.quote: [p.226] The suprasegmental systems are relatively complicated and manifest themselves in complex stress systems with rhythm patterns, and a two-tone system is present in all the languages, except apparently in Wabuda. Its functional load appears to be low in all the languages except for North-Eastern Kiwai and (Arigibi ?) where it seems to be quite high. [p.242, on Bamu Kiwai] In other respects, Bamu Kiwai phonology is much more like that of other Kiwaian languages than that of Wabuda. Long vowels are rare, and a two-tone system appears to be present.
new_statements.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 1973. The Kiwaian language family. In Karl J. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea, 217-260. Pacific Linguistics C-26. Canberra: Research School of Pacific Studies, ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-C26.217
new_statements.locator: p.226, sec. 6.51 'Phonology' (family-level, PDF page 10); p.242, sec. 6.63.4 'Notes on Bamu Kiwai' (PDF page 26)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress placement is given. Wurm's survey says every Kiwaian language including Bamu Kiwai has a 'complex stress system with rhythm patterns' plus a two-tone system of low functional load, and specifically that Bamu Kiwai 'appears' to have a two-tone system; the position of word stress is not stated anywhere.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (only 'rhythm patterns' at family level).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Bamu; Wabuda is said to lack the two-tone system; tone has high functional load in North-Eastern Kiwai (and Arigibi?).
new_statements.domain_note: Family-level typological summary (sec. 6.51) explicitly covering all Kiwaian languages; the Bamu-specific paragraph (sec. 6.63.4) is based on Ray 1923, Wurm 1951, Capell 1962, Riley & Ray 1930-31, Voorhoeve's Middle Bamu materials and Wurm's own Sisiame field notes. Word-level phonology; no phrase/citation-form distinction discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Bamu = Bamu Kiwai (Glottolog bamu1257, ISO bcf), which Wurm 1973 (sec. 6.63) divides into Sisiame (main, c. 2,850 speakers), Pirupiru/Gama (c. 850) and Middle Bamu (c. 700; the mission standard, Scripture 1952) dialects; Riley & Ray's vocabularies are Sisiame (with Oropai) and Pirupiru, Ray 1913-14 has Sisiami and Buniki (= Dibiri), Wurm's own notes are Sisiame, and the Carr & Carr dictionary labels forms Odi / Humo. The quoted p.226 statement is a family-level generalisation over all Kiwaian languages; only the p.242 tone sentence is Bamu-specific.

sources.citation: Carr, Chris & Phil Carr. 2011. Bamu Dictionary. [Draft, OpenOffice source 'BamuDictJun11.rtf' dated 15/06/11; 94 pp., entries A-W.] SIL Papua New Guinea. (Glottolog 314566)
sources.note: Alphabetical entries only; no introduction, orthography or phonology section; no stress marks. The only prosodic notes are the entry 'a INTERJ... Low tone seeks agreement, high tone is accusing' (p.1) and a few headwords with a capital-A/colon phonetic gloss (tapi tA:pi, sabi sA:bi, kakisa kA:kisA, papamo pApA:mo). Uses dialect labels Odi / Humo. fetched sources from https://archive.org/details/bamudictionary (third-party upload 2019).

sources.note: Bamu Kiwai (Sisiame) cited only for syntax examples (negative marker follows the verb; object sometimes follows verb). Kiwaian family paragraph repeats the 'complex stress system... two-tone system' summary. No position.
Empty placeholder ('This text is in the process of being added'). Nothing.
No phonology content; cites only Ethnologue 25 and a UN village-coordinates dataset.

sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 1971. Notes on the linguistic situation in the Trans-Fly area. In Dutton, Voorhoeve & Wurm (eds.), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 14, 115-172. Pacific Linguistics A-28. DOI 10.15144/PL-A28.115
sources.note: Sec. 3.31.13 Bamu Kiwai (pp.137-138): speakers, dialects, sources, loss of intervocalic consonants, simplified morphology; no stress statement for Bamu. Family-level Kiwai paragraph repeats 'complex stress system with rhythm principles, and a two-tone system... functional load extremely low'. No position.

sources.citation: Riley, E. Baxter & Sidney H. Ray. 1930-1931. Sixteen vocabularies from the Fly River, Papua. Anthropos 25: 173-193, 831-850; 26: 171-192.
sources.note: Sisiame (with Oropai) and Pirupiru vocabularies. Ray's 'Notes on the vocabularies. A. Phonology' (26: 190-191) lists consonants/vowels/diphthongs, a hiatus sign, dialect sound correspondences, 'every consonant is followed by a vowel'. No stress/accent statement (the only 'accent' is a dialect-difference remark on Wabuda at Gesoa, 25: 174). archive.org scans of the volumes.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1923. The languages of the Western Division of Papua. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute 53: 332-360. DOI 10.2307/2843574
sources.note: Lists Sisiami, Dibiri (Buniki) and Pirupiru as Kiwai-group localities (p.335); 'Note on orthography' (p.336) just refers to RGS spelling rules; 'Notes on grammar' (pp.337ff) cover nouns, pronouns, verbs. Silent on stress/accent. archive.org (Digital Library of India) scan dli.ministry.15591.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1913-1914. The languages of the Papuan Gulf District, Papua. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 4: 20-67.
sources.note: Sisiami and Buniki vocabularies (from Riley) with grammatical notes; only 'Alphabet... vowels are to be pronounced as in German, the consonants as in English' (p.22). Silent on stress. archive.org (Toronto) scan afrikaundberse0401meinuoft.
